title: AI #191: The Hackening Begins
summary: It was the probably worst day in cybersecurity history. So far. Not only is there a critical flaw in PHP that due to a leak was announced a day before the fix would be available, sending most of the internet scrambling for solutions and likely dooming a lot of long tail websites permanently, there were several other unrelated incidents. The floodgates seem to have been opened. I have a market on whether there will be
source: Zvi · Don't Worry About the Vase
body:
It was the probably worst day in cybersecurity history. So far. Not only is there a critical flaw in PHP that due to a leak was announced a day before the fix would be available, sending most of the internet scrambling for solutions and likely dooming a lot of long tail websites permanently, there were several other unrelated incidents. The floodgates seem to have been opened. I have a market on whether there will be an even worse day before the end of the year .

Another key leak this week was the draft bill Anthropic had been shopping around Congress , similar to but weaker than the FRONTIER Act. Anthropic’s initial attempts to explain itself only made the situation seem worse, as they seemed to not understand the problem with what they had done. Dario’s later response was better, but the situation remains troubling. There are enough different Anthropic developments, that I plan to have a post soon covering them all. It is a mix of news running from excellent to terrible.

Will interpretability save us ? There is a new claim that neural networks are cleaner than we thought, meaning that individual neurons mostly have a single interpretable meaning, and it is tractable to go through and label them one by one. Initial reactions got out of hand, treating this as a far bigger development than it was. This is still excellent news that makes our estimate of difficulty substantially lower going forward. The work can begin.

We had better get on that, because there have been quite a few misalignment incidents .

I continue to owe a write-up of the Gemini 4 Argon Safety Card. That is in progress and hopefully I will finish it soon. Life has gotten in the way. I may or may not have a full capabilities report on Gemini 4 Argon once I tally up the reactions. Muse Wonder definitely will not have such a post, as it has proven to have been oversold.

- Language Models Offer Mundane Utility.

- Language Models Don’t Offer Mundane Utility.

- Get My Agent On The Line.

- Deepfaketown and Botpocalypse Soon.

- Fun With Media Generation.

- A Young Lady’s Illustrated Primer.

- Bubble, Bubble, Toil and Trouble.

- Quickly, There’s No Time.

- The Quest for Sane Regulations.

- DeepMind Made Him Sign an NDA.

- OpenAI Sells Out On Chips.

- People Just Say Things.

- Rhetorical Innovation.

- Maybe You Should Quit.

- The American People Really Hate AI.

- Aligning a Smarter Than Human Intelligence is Difficult.

- Cooperative Alignment.

- Marc Andreessen Hulk Smash.

- People Are Worried About AI Killing Everyone.

Automate proving to your incompetent building that yes, you have paid the rent .

Find the first use of ECDSA . Claude found the seeds .

AI models confirmed good at econometric coding in particular .

58% of Anthropic staff expect Claude to make a Nobel prize level scientific discovery by 2027. I agree with Roon that this should have been over 95% . The event itself might not be over 95% to happen, but it has to be a clear favorite to happen, so it is crazy for so many employees to not agree with that.

Tell you what you actually want to know straight up.

PoliMath : Me: How long should I bake chicken wings

Google top result: “When I first proposed that we start a backyard coop, my husband was deeply reticent (5 pages later) Anyway, here is our recipe for honey mustard chicken wings”

AI: Bake at 425 for 40-50 minutes

Vibe code your fraud.gov website , probably using Opus 4.8. Which is fine, so long as you do a decent job of it.

PoIiMath : The AI was wrong.

Yes, of course the AIs will be ‘more accurate’ to the law plus underlying ground truth, but if we wanted accuracy we would not use typical juries .

Robin Hanson : Whenever you put AIs in charge of something important, you have to wonder how the firms which make them will respond to various pressures from powerful parties to slant their AIs in particular directions.

The point of a jury is to provide a check on the system and avoid abuses or overly strict adherence to the letter of the law, and to protect the innocent and our rights, not to be accurate. Judges are a much superior accuracy tech. Thus, an AI jury (or one AI judge) does not solve your problem. What you likely want is a human jury that has the ability to query AIs. They can override that, but have to do it on purpose.

If you read AI writing , you can then talk to the author in some sense, or read their further thoughts, but not in the sense that Tyler Cowen would like.

Claude Duet is the Claude answer to other proactive agents like Muse and Dot. It uses Opus 5.5 and is now in early research preview through a waitlist.

DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 exists . Their benchmark chart contains Opus 5 and 5.6 Sol. It’s probably a solid upgrade over the old V4.1-Flash anyway, but wow.

How did it come to exist? One guess.

Lisan al Gaib : very curious that DeepSeek now has the same terse reasoning style as Astra. must be a coincidence.

Dean W. Ball : Distillation has always been part of the explanation for why China is so close behind the U.S. in model benchmark performance. But one of my updates after joining openai is that distillation probably plays a bigger role in the explanation than I realized.

I haven’t really shared this publicly because people will next-token complete the obvious cope “buhhhh you are just saying that because derrrr” replies but it really is true, regardless of whether you think it’s good or not.

I would have guessed distillation explained ~30% of Chinese close-behindness before seeing what one can see within openai, and after that, more like 50%.

Opus 5.5 fast mode available for everyone in the Claude Platform at 8/40 . You get up to a 2.5x speedup.

OpenAI expands access to GPT-Rosalind for scientific research .

OpenAI models are coming to Google Cloud.

OpenAI offers us GPT-Live-1.1 including new voices in various languages.

Muse Spark Open exists , as in a version of Muse Spark is now an open model . They call it ‘the most capable US open-weight model to date.’ That seems likely to be true. It scores a 39 on Artificial Analysis. The open weight frontier for that index is 46 for MiMo-V2.6-Pro and Qwen-3.8, and MiMo is a lot cheaper to run than Muse Spark. Nathan Lambert calls this his ‘super bowl,’ says this closes the gap substantially, and points to the Interconnects Adoption Dashboard where Spark is #8. This is not a fair competition, since the Chinese can do Massive Fraudulent Distillation, whereas Meta does many things but it won’t do that .

There are some advantages to having a semi-competitive American open model. I wouldn’t say that I trust Meta, but you can use their models in places where you would not be comfortable running Chinese models, even locally.

Lack of upgrades: There was no major Chinese open weights release between September 21 and October 16. No DeepSeek, GLM, Kimi, MiMo or Qwen.

Nathan Lambert (I asked him why no releases): Compute restrictions, I do think there’s more internal lab-govt discussions on safety in China, less organization development. No good answers, but I’ve been monitoring & pondering

We then got a new DeepSeek, but no version number increment, on October 17.

One theory is this is a random lull. Another is that Anthropic and OpenAI improved their distillation defenses, and the Chinese are stuck.

The Muse Wonder model card is here . Is it a good model, sir?

Meta certainly claims it is. Their pitch, although they don’t say the line, is full ‘ introducing the world’s most powerful model .’ The term quoted in Bloomberg is ‘Meta says new Muse model hits AI frontier .’

They even have an explicit line and supposed test about not “benchmaxxing.”

Alexandr Wang : MUSE WONDER

muse wonder is the best model in the world for personal agents and professional agents.

we evaluated our model against the best models in the world across agentic and coding tasks, and we think you all will like it.

Some quick responses were very positive.

Eleanor Berger : Used the not full version for only a little bit and it’s definitely very good. Like previous Muse models, it’s better in written text and interaction than all other models. And it’s very fast and smart and agentic. Time to start taking Meta seriously as a frontier AI lab.

Theo (this was before Argon was available): My current model rankings

S – Opus 5.5, Muse Wonder

Kelsey Piper : I think it’s more narrowly a coding model than the latest Claude and ChatGPT offerings. It’s markedly worse (both on benchmarks and in use) at research and writing.

My reaction thread had only two responses overnight , one of them asking for the safety report and the other saying it was similar to Grok 4.7.

Same as it ever was. Meta is making progress, but is still solidly behind the frontier.

Meta also reinforced its reputation for overselling and being untrustworthy. Once again, they have misrepresented a new release. Claims of things like ‘best model in the world’ for personal agents and professional agents’ are clearly false.

Kelsey Piper on some current AI writing capability failures:

Kelsey Piper : Even frontier models have poor theory of mind, they suck at having characters know something and not say it without the narration directly telling to to you anyway. This is crippling for espionage/detective stories in particular

They’re very mechanical when trying to convert one story to a different format, or else have bad judgment about which details need including. Salience/importance is hard for them.

Their characters all talk the same or else like exaggerated caricatures of themselves. They’re really bad at the kind of subtle humor that makes the infodump parts of eg Tom Clancy keep from stalling out

Epoch reconstructs videos of runs for SpireClimb , their Slay the Spire benchmark, that speeds them up enough to be watchable .

Win rates for Ascension 0 are now very high, yes ‘top human’ level is close to 100%:

Ascension 20 (max difficulty) is much harder. You do not win ‘by accident’ or by taking generically good cards. This is a higher win rate than I expected to see so soon and Sol and Astra are doing much better than the average player, even confined to those who unlocked max difficulty and choose to play it.

Slay the Spire 2 also sees the models struggle at max difficulty (A10), but yes it is easier right now and you can sometimes get lucky.

Is this a coincidence or is it deliberate training? The working theory is a mix of both.

Thomas Friedel : do you think OpenAI had a RL env to train Astra specifically for STS ? Performance is unbelievably high. Higher than my dedicated STS2 model.

Benjamin Ou : Benchmark creator here! Probably yeah, GPT generations have gotten ridiculously strong at this while not necessarily being as strong on easier games like EBR-bench, and other models are pretty far behind. We know the labs like the game, so all signs point to RL.

Not to downplay how strong they’re getting in general at strategy card games other than StS though, there’s def some generalization going on as well.

Opus 5.5 does scarily well on ChildhoodBench , as in correctly predicting major outcomes for Jack based on his childhood writings.

HouseholdBench asks models to predict household spending behavior . Models can reduce error by ~12% versus a baseline of no changes. Open weight models lag.

#### Choose Your Fighter

I continue to see many reports like this, whereas months ago people said the opposite:

Utah teapot : kinda weird how a week worth of gpt 500 seems to get about as much done as 5 hours of claude 200.

UPS blocks AI agents . So do for example Delta , JP Morgan Chase, Charles Schwab and Amazon. The group doing this by default is going to keep expanding. The agents will still be useful, but less so.

The biggest other practical barrier for agents like Dots , and also many new Claude projects, is overrefusals and misclassifications that require permissions. This is a hard problem, since the other error is worse. As an example, I gave my Dot a ‘do not delete anything that does not have source control’ rule before trying anything else, and it took that to some rather extreme places. Claude auto mode asking for permission so often is actively less safe than if it asked less, because many users will quickly stop even reading the requests.

If you share a Muse conversation it can get indexed and end up in the public records. In general it seems fair to assume that if you share an AI conversation there is a good chance the link will get indexed, so if you’re not okay with that then don’t share it directly.

Patrick McKenzie gets first exposure to multi-agent development workflows , agrees it is obviously the future and will eat infinite tokens, and other unsurprising thoughts.

Patrick McKenzie : It is deeply weird to, in the middle of extremely productive work, have a long argument with a coordination process attempting to argue with a subagent.

The exact contents of the hour-long argument I will not recount, but at about thirty minutes in I was wondering how anything capable of writing software code could be so obtuse. About an hour in I thought “Oh I am not first ~CEO to have this thought am I.”

In practice deepfakes continue to not be a substantial practical problem. Politicians still care if you enable them. It is one of the easy bad things to understand.

Chris Sommerfeldt : [NYC] Council Speaker Julie Menin tells SpaceXAI’s Gabriela Castillo Madrid she created a sexualized image of herself using Grok. She asks how that’s possible if Grok has sufficient controls.

“I’m happy to have our safety team look into that specific instance,” Castillo Madrid says.

After the hearing, Menin says she’ll “definitely” follow up with SpaceXAI about this because she wasn’t satisfied with the testimony. She also says Castillo Madrid was “lying” when she claimed she didn’t know about the firing of a SpaceXAI employee who raised security concerns.

Stanford race-swaps (and gender-swaps) students in advertising, and also to slim down and alter faces. The Stanford Review’s Zayd Patel then suggested this was good , because if you fabricate diversity using AI then that beats doing it in practice. That seems to have led to a Title VI complaint against the paper .

What happens if AIs can launch frivolous lawsuits? Defense is far from free.

Ethan Mollick : A consequential choice will be made soon by government and companies as they are increasingly flooded with agentic AI inquiries that overcome the frictions that gated access (see the graphs – it has already started!)

Two options: do you make services worse or better as a result?

Status quo isn’t an option. You can either add additional frictions (adding fees, make services worse, ban agents) or remove them (provide more services with AI help, redesign work to make access easier). Paper [here] .

Flo Crivello : Seeing this in my circles — several founder friends have told me they’ve started getting hit with a huge amount of frivolous lawsuits

Dean W. Ball : It’ll be interesting in particular if people feel they can self-represent when launching frivolous lawsuits. Lawyers can be punished or suffer reputational damage for truly egregious frivolity, but a non-lawyer cares less about these things.

You do both. The good news is that there are ways to ‘make it worse’ that do not do that much damage to legitimate users.

The modern world already has a bunch of scammers and other predatory humans, and algorithms, out there trying to get people’s money or attention. A lot of people are not equipped to deal with things even as they are now. We feared AI would supercharge all that. It took longer than expected, and so far such effects have been rare, but it will happen more often over time. It will no longer be a news story that ‘ Bricklayer, 49, travels 1,200 miles for dream girl – only to discover she’s AI-generated .’

Pangram could attempt to make an AI that ‘writes like a human,’ but won’t . That does not mean it would write like a ‘good’ human writer either way.

Yes, some people are lying scum who will present AI-written stories as real in order to drum up outrage. This is a demand-driven problem. The AI makes faking the story easier, but it also makes the fake stories easier to catch. Blame the human, not the AI.

Kelsey Piper : Half a million views, tons of right wing posters like this one going “when we talk about cultural compatibility it’s not some hypothetical issue”, and no one asked “is that letter entirely AI generated” (yes) and “is it in fact almost the exact letter you get if you say ‘generate a fake HOA letter telling me to stop smoking brisket’ (yes), “would a first class letter dated Saturday October 17 arrive in time to complain about it bright and early Monday morning” (no), “is the letter consistent with Arizona laws around notice periods” (no), “how many HOAs in Arizona have a nuisance provision 8.4” (5, according to ChatGPT), and “do any of them employ a Marjorie” (no).

I continue not to understand how restaurants end up using AI images of food when they have real food you can photograph. Do people actually prefer it this way? I suppose many of them do.

Update on the OpenAI spy : Yes he used his wife’s ChatGPT to plan planting the bug. There were at least two recording devices. He was in communication with a member of the Saudi royal family and there are additional clear signs that his client was the Saudi government. There’s also this:

Kevin Khadavi : My investigation into the alleged OpenAI spy’s Stanford ties got 126k views, but the response seemed unusually negative. I decided to look into it: the overwhelming majority of accounts attacking my reporting are Saudi.

The good news is that OpenAI is giving its employees anti-honeypot training , as in to watch out that those trying to seduce them might be spies.

I like to think that Anthropic employees get similar training, except they also are told not to talk about it. If not, get on that, guys. Same for the other labs too.

unusual_whales : BREAKING: OpenAI is warning its employees to watch out for spies, especially romantic ones, per WSJ

The company has cautioned staff that someone trying to seduce them may likely be a “honeypot.”

Even strangers approaching them in everyday places could be gathering info.

Georgia Wells, Erin Woo and Meghan Bobrowsky (The Wall Street Journal): One story OpenAI tells employees to illustrate the risk: To seduce a U.S. diplomat in Russia, a foreign espionage operation first sent a blond woman to his hotel room with Champagne. When he declined, the spies sent a redheaded woman, and then next a young man. The implication for OpenAI employees was this could happen to them, according to the people.

I like to think that if I was a diplomat, by the time I see the second unknown hottie show up at my hotel room with Champagne I would be pretty confident it was a trap. There are many things that are much more effective on their first try. Mix it up a little.

Kelsey Piper : I worry this makes things really hard for extremely attractive people who just want to seduce an OpenAI or Anthropic employee for their money.

Andrew Rettek : And they’re the real victims here.

Kelsey Piper : imagine being engaged in the innocent and time-honored trad pastime of marrying the richest guy you can find and being accused of international espionage just because you are really really hot.

alice : i personally want to seduce them for their extremely accurate meows

What changed is that we noticed the problem. The problem has existed for a while.

Zack Korman : The OpenAI employee who allegedly stole over a hundred confidential documents without OpenAI noticing for months sent the documents to his number *in mainland China*

This is all a big problem in its own right. If you cannot protect your secrets from spies, including the Chinese, then there is no point in trying to ‘win the race.’

This is also indicative of other problems. If you cannot solve your employee misalignment problems, how are you going to solve AI misalignment problems?

The first best way to learn with Claude is very different from ‘create practice sheets and teacher updates’ but it is a vast upgrade on similar actions without Claude.

cold : Kids these days are getting tiger parented by Claude

Jack : this rocks, in fact

I’m feeling out a Take that if a tutor is not using AI in their work at this point, they are veering towards negligence, because tutor+AI now dominates tutor alone at ~all levels of competence

Vladislav Ekimtcov : claude obsoletes school tbh. you can do an entire k-12 in a single github monorepo with fun little widgets that teach how to write every letter and add up numbers

Is AI changing the world? Freddie deBoer says no , ‘ human life in 2026 appears to be almost entirely similar to human life in 2021 .’ Jack disagrees, pointing out that all his friends and family have had their jobs transformed.

Jack : Five years of AI has changed the world dramatically more than five years of electricity or five years of the combustion engine did. It’s not even close.

AI so far has simultaneously changed the world more than any other technology (at least if you exclude military techs that won active wars) in its first five years. AI so far has also changed the world dramatically less than I or many others would have expected in that time, if we had been told the path of AI capabilities. Diffusion takes time and a lot of things have been bottlenecked.

As AI use continues to grow exponentially, expect bigger impacts, with the impact growing faster all the time, even if capabilities mostly stop improving from here.

Anthropic is hiring for a smaller share of junior positions and AI agent hours outnumber employee hours six to one . Human attention is a bottleneck for AI outputs and human productivity is way up. That’s the central finding of a new Anthropic report on what it is like to work there.

Anthropic : At the same time, the overall employment share of technical departments within Anthropic has fallen, from 61% to 56% in the last year. As the company expands, technical hiring has continued growing in absolute terms, but intensive hiring in sales, finance, and recruiting has outpaced it.

… Even clerical work tightly connected to in-person interaction has grown slowly. An executive assistant, who built a personal assistant agent for scheduling and email triage, explained: “I think we’ve already moved past the point of Claude augmenting away the really entry-level admin type role,” and instead focused their work on higher-order “chief of staff” tasks.

These changes have already involved reallocation: employees working at the company for at least a year were 50% more likely to move across departments each month in 2026 than they were in 2025.

They have a chart for ‘reading Claude as a full time job.’

Some think that soon either the jobs be gone or the jobs be fake.

EigenGender : There is simply no future where humans continue to do economically useful work for much longer. Your choice is at best between various flavors of “ASI let’s humans have fun and play make believe.”

(to be clear this is a good thing!)

Opinions are very strong on whether or not this would, if it happens, be a good thing. In some ways it is very good. In others it is very bad.

Anatoly Karlin : I strongly believe that everyone countersignaling against post-scarcity utopia on the basis of the “dignity” and “sanctity” of work should have do a lengthy stint as a Dhaka garments factory or African subsistence farmer. Talk is cheap from the air conditioned ivory tower.

Jack : I very strongly want a world where humans continue to pursue meaningful expertise and accomplishment, but I think Karlin is right that a lot of dignity-of-work takes come from people who have the uncommon luxury of dignified work.

Some view not having real work as being kind of AI pets (you are the pet, pejorative).

Linus Mixson : I suspect it’s as non-obvious to most people as it is to me that “ASI pets” is a more desirable future than is extinction, and I think it’s worth straightforwardly confronting the fact that Anthropic, both as a collective and at the level of its individual constituents, seems to think it rather decisively is.

Aleph : This has always seemed obviously wrong to me. If you ask the average person if they would prefer they and their family be murdered to living forever in a world of AI abundance they’re going to laugh at you. Absurd to believe otherwise.

Most talk of ‘pets for the AI’ is nonsense, but the answer to ‘does humans continuing to exist in abundance (or even adequacy) without needing to do productive work constitute a net positive future’ seems to obviously be yes. It might not be the ideal path, but the hard part is making that future have an equilibrium of that type, not coming up with net positive experiences.

You can go work for a Congressman on AI. Seems impactful.

Congressman Nathaniel Moran : My office is hiring an Artificial Intelligence Policy Fellow to help shape AI legislation and track AI developments in the private sector as Congress works to keep pace with the technology.

Experience in AI, policy research, or national security is encouraged.

Not AI, but if you know anyone who wants to hire Terese, she’s awesome.

Terese : I’m looking for work as a wet lab biologist in the San Francisco Bay Area. My PhD was in genetics and neuroscience but I’m open to exploring new fields. I’ve only ever been in academia, so if you do wet lab work in biotech, I’d love to hear what it’s like! DMs open.

Jakeup : I dragged my wife to SF from a post doc at a Nobel laureate’s lab at Columbia with the promise of cool Bay Area biotech. Cool Bay Area biotech, this is your chance to snap her up.

From October 8: OSS Scanner from Anthropic , which offers free, periodic opt-in security scans for open-source projects .

Utah Teapot estimates only 35k-69k people working in AI, total, from all angles .

Citrini Research goes to Anthropic’s offices to try and tell Claude to do a medical breakthrough, make no mistakes. Early results are promising and they conclude the frontier has moved, but you still have to test the ideas the old fashioned way.

Microsoft publishes a detailed report on how they did a new 3T-size pre-training . Their presentation includes chart crimes. This seems like a ‘those who know shouldn’t tell and those who tell don’t know’ style of report. Claude’s analysis is that they are still not so close to the frontier, but that this is plausibly something they can usefully license or use for recruitment, and that it has minimal uplift value.

Simons Foundation launched 15 million effort to help mathematics navigate the AI era, including contributions from Anthropic (5 million) and OpenAI.

China is ‘cramming for the AI revolution ,’ with many investing in learning to use AI . The Chinese people are (correctly) terrified of being left behind and not having a place in the future, and have a long tradition of turning to education.

FTC sends extensive civil investigative demands to Anthropic and OpenAI , as expected.

Take a minute to reflect on what the news sounds like these days, versus how sci-fi it would have sounded like two years ago . It is so easy to become numb.

j⧉nus : daily news always like dis now

Ethan Mollick wrote a book, Co-Existence , about how to live and work in a world where AI is sometimes, but not always, better than you.

Coverage of Anthropic’s financials will be in the Anthropic post later this week.

Jensen Huang is excellent at making chips, not so good at public statements.

Polymarket : JUST IN: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang assures investors the AI stock selloff is temporary, declaring, “All of this is going to pass.”

Let us say my sentiment about AI stocks did not go up hearing that sentence.

DeepSeek raises 15 billion .

Microsoft cancels UK data center deal with Nscale , in part over power concerns.

Anthropic in talks for a 45 billion cloud computing deal with Nscale . A classic your loss is our gain scenario, perhaps. Nscale is trying to IPO and lost the Microsoft project, so Anthropic should be able to press for a good deal.

NYC comptroller calls on Anthropic to pause its public offering ‘until it has fully addressed risks around artificial intelligence,’ as in permanently. He has no power over this decision, but he has thoughts.

Meta ordered to pay 25 billion penalty in New Mexico Cambridge Analytica case , as the judge found Meta’s deception to be intentional and did not take kindly to that. Many other states collectively settled for far less.

Trump has confirmed distribution via the Trump accounts and there is talk that OpenAI might do something similar.

SpaceX shares are trading around 146, so if all the shares are transferred Elon Musk could be granting around 10 billion. That is real money.

Giving the shares to the public sounds cool. It does not make economic sense, and the transaction costs will be high, and it does nothing to make us not die despite Musk thinking we might all die. It still might be the best option.

The reason you do it that way is symbolic, and to maybe give people the idea that they are ‘invested in’ SpaceX’s success. If that’s what gets him the motivation to do it, and how it can happen and avoid government taking a stake, then great. Second best help is still help.

Returning to Anthropic, my biggest concern is that the Benefit Fund, like many employees, will not focus on making AI go well and having everyone not die, and instead choose less impactful causes. The only action they rule out is ‘lobbying or political giving.’ Yes, offering funds to buffer against economic disruption is a noble cause, but a secondary one, and trying to fix that privately is an infinite money sink.
summaryZh: AI #191：黑客攻击开始。这可能是网络安全历史上最糟糕的一天。 PHP 不仅存在一个严重缺陷，由于在修复程序可用的前一天宣布了泄漏，导致大多数互联网都在争夺解决方案，并可能导致许多长尾网站永久灭亡，而且还发生了其他几起不相关的事件。
